                                              RAJYA SABHA                            [7 August, 2000] 
Government's Opposition to disinvestment of Government equity in 
certain PSUs 
 *202. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of HEAVY INDUSTRIES 
AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that Government had opposed the disinvestment of Government 
equity in certain PSUs on the ground that they are of a strategic manner; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any decision has been taken by G overnment in terms of properly defining 
strategic and non-strategic sectors; and 
(d) if so, when and other details thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING, MINISTER 
OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME 
IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE MINISTRY OF 
PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PE NSIONS AND MINISTER OF STATE 
OF THE DEPARTMENT OF DI SINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (d) A 
statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The decisions in regard to the ge neral disinvestment policy or the disinvestment 
proposals in specific PSUs are taken by the Gove rnment after inter ministerial consultation 
at various levels. 
 All the concerned departments a nd ministries express their views OP the 
proposals under consideration and often suggest ame ndments and   improvements   to   the   
proposals.    These   suggestions   for amendmentsimprovements are duly considered by 
Government at the time of taking final decisions. 
(c) and (d) The Government has clearly defined the strategic and 
2 

[7 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
non-strategic Public Sector Enterprises as per the decision dated 16-3-99. The definition is that 
the Strategic Public Sector Enterprises would be those in the areas of: 
1. Arms and ammunitions and the allied items of defence equipments, defence 
aircrafts and warships. 
2. Atomic Energy (except in the areas related to the generation of nuclear power and 
applications of radiation and radio-isotopes agriculture medicine and non-strategic 
industries). 
3. Railway Transport 
It was also decided that for the non-strategic Public Sector Enterprises, the reduction of 
Government share to 26% would not be automatic and the manner and pace of doing so 
would be worked out keeping in mind the circumstances of the sector and company in 
question. A decision in regard to the percentage of disinvestment i.e., Government share 
going down to less than 51% or to 26% would be taken on the following 
considerations: 
(a) Whether the Industrial Sector requires the presence of the public sector as a 
countervailing force to prevent concentration of power in private hands, and 
(b) Whether the Industrial sector requires a proper regulatory mechanism to protect the 
consumer interests before Public Sector Enterprises are privatised. 
 SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Sir, frankly speaking, we are confused because in the 
Press, there have been widespread reports. The Ministry of Heavy Industries has said that power 
is one of the sectors which is strategic, in terms of country's economic development. Now, 
Bharat Heavy Electrical Ltd. which is a premier organisation and one of the Navratnas, has done 
wonderfully well, not only within the country but in terms of global competition also. When the 
Navratna package was announced, it was understood that these companies will get support to 
become global competitors. The biggest problem in this area is that, in spite of the fact that these 
are very good companies because of the financial package that these companies have to offer as 
part of the bidding process globally, they 
3 

                                              RAJYA SABHA      [7 August, 2000] 
are outsmarted by some of these multinational companies from the West and other 
developed companies. Therefore, we learn—there  were Press reports—that the Ministry of 
Heavy Industries has argued—and logically—within the Government, for continuation of 
BHEL in the public sector and for not going in for the disinvestment route. But, here, we see 
that it has not been considered. So, would th e hon. Minister be kind enough to elaborate 
this? Why a company like BHEL is not treated as stretegic company and considered for 
disinvestment? 
 SHRI ARUN SHOURIE: Sir, classifi cation of strategic and non-strategic 
industries is based on the report of the Disinve stment Commission wherein they have listed 
that there were to be only four categories of industries which were to be regarded as strategic. 
These were first, defence-related industries; second atomic energy; third, minerals related to 
atomic energy; and fourth, railways. This is on page 17 of the 1st Volume of the 
Disinvestment Commission's report. Exactly this categorisation was adopted by the 
Government, except that the Ministry of Indus try itself and the De partment of Atomic 
Energy suggested that on the third item, that is, the classification of  minerals or beachsand 
required for atomic energy, the earlier Atomic Energy Control Order of 1953 had been 
subsequently amended in 19 5, and so, that h ead should not be there, other heads should be 
tlure. So, those three categories of defence-re lated industries, atom ic energy and some 
related minerals—not all—and railways were re garded as strategic. So, I don't see any 
ambiguity in that. Secondly, on this classification, as I explained, during the extensive debate 
on disinvestment spread over two days, it had been adopted by the Government in March 
1999 and it has been reiterated many times. That is the classification that is there today. 
 SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Sir, it is quite amusing. It almost sounds like the devil 
quoting the scriptures because, earlier when there was a debate on this subject in this House 
itself, a number of examples were quoted by hon. Members that certain very meaningful 
recommendations of the Disinvestment Commission did not get the kind of consideration by 
the Government that it deserved in this pa rticular area. Now, the question is how the 
classification has come; 
4 

[7 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
what is its genesis and what is the logic? For example, you take the case of oil sector PSUs. 
After Independence, we had a situation when the entire western oil companies withdrew 
from the country saying that the oil sector had no  viability; therefore, they totally withdrew 
their investment; and the country was totall y dependent on imports for its oil needs. 
Therefore, the genesis of what should be a strategic sector and which companies will be 
strategic also depends on the history of the c ountry and the experience which we develop. 
From that standpoint, I just fail to unders tand how a company like BHEL cannot be treated 
as a strategic company. Therefore, I would like to know, through you, Sir, from the Minister 
as to why companies which are related to the food security of the country, or, companies 
which help us in reducing our dependence on tota l import of oil, or strategic companies like 
BHEL are not treated as strategic companies. Will the Minister elaborate on that because 
the recommendations of the Disinvestment Commission, by itself, cannot be the logic? 
 SHRI ARUN SHOURIE: Sir, if I may kindl y draw your attention to the question 
itself, it says, "(a) whether it is a fact that the Government had opposed the disinvestment of 
Government equity in certain PSUs..." The Government is, certainly, not opposing whatever 
it is proposing to do. That is the question. It is  on the general categorisation of industries, if 
we are to discuss specific sectors, or firm s like BHEL, or, oil companies, and so on, 
probably, that should be the subject of a sepa rate question. I can, certainly answer it now, 
but it will take some time. 
 Secondly, even in cases of sectors or  firms which have been regarded as non-
strategic, the Government has said that disinvestment in them will not be automatic. 
Disinvestment in them will be subjected to two criteria, which the Government will Assess. 
One of them is whether the continuance of the public sector in that industry is necessary so 
as to prevent market dominance by one firm; whet her it is a foreign firm  or an Indian firm. 
That is, certainly, very much in the mind of government in the case of oil sector and many 
other sectors. 
 Sir, the second criterion which has been laid down is, even if it is  
5 

                                                       RAJYA SABHA          [7 August, 2000] 
not going to result in market dominance, whether that sector requires a proper regulatory 
mechanism before the public sector withdraws. All these precautions have been taken and will 
be observed in this matter. Certainly, in the case of oil, whether it is ONGC or Oil India or the 
distribution companies and so on, all these factors are going to be kept in mind. But, Sir, if you 
direct that we should take up the individual cases, I have the material; and I can, certainly, go 
into that.

part 2 of the answer is with regard to the cl assification of atomic energy. The answer says

elements and the third is value-adding process.  Last year a global te nder was invited by the 
Department of Atomic Energy for the proce ss of mining. My specific question to the hon. 
Minister is whether any proposal is pending for any of these activities, namely, separation of 
mineral elements etc. through the value adding process, especially by the IRE Limited. 
 SHRI ARUN SHOURIE: Sir, as I mentioned,  in the original classification these 
items have been split in two; one was atomic energy and the second was minerals specified 
in the Schedule to the Atomic Energy Control, Production and Use Order, 1953. This is how 
the classification had been put in the original note about the strategic sector. On this the 
Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion concurred with the new classification which 
had been proposed and which is exactly this. But they pointed out that that Order of 1953 
had been amended by the Department of Atomic Energy's Notification of 15th March, 1995. 
The Department of Atomic Energy went fu rther and pointed out that actually the 
exploitation of beach sand had already been opened up by the Government of India for the 
private sector, including foreign direct investment, up to 74 per cent. They also said that this 
terminology should be changed and that it is not necessary to retain the entry 'minerals 
specified in Schedule of 1953.' Further it suggested that the entry 'atomic energy' about which 
the hon. Member asked, may be modified to read, 'atomic energy except in the areas related 
to the generation of nuclear power and the applications of radiation and radioisotopes to 
agriculture, medicine and non-strategic industries.' That is the exact proposal, Sir, that was 
made by the Department of Atomic Energy, and that is the exact wording adopted by the 
Cabinet in its classification. As to whethe r there is a new proposal on those types of 
minerals and so on, Sir, that is a question th at would probably be better addressed to the 
Department of Atomic Energy. Sir, if you so direct, I will get this information from the 
Department and give it to the hon. Member.

Disinvestment Commission has made its recommendation. I will read it out to you. They

sell a minimum of 51 per cent of its current holding to a strategic buyer with transfer of

Commission further went on to say, "After the induction of a strategic buyer and completion 
of on-going modernisation progra mmes, Government could eventually disinvest its balance 
holding in NFL through a public offer of shares to domestic institutions and retail investors." 
So, Sir, certainly, Government is aware not only of Dr. Nanjundappa's note, but also of the a 
view that was taken eventually by the Disinvestment

INDUSTRY (SHRI DR. RAMAN): (a) Yes, sir. 
 (b) to (d) Patents are granted under the soverign prerogative of c ountries according to 
their respective Patent Laws and have territorial effect, that is, they are effective only in the 
country of grant. However, as and when information is received about patents being obtained on 
certain items which are not considered patentable and which affect Indian interests, steps are 
taken to assess whether the grant of such patent can be challenged under the patent laws of the 
country concerned. 
 Earlier a patent granted in the United States of America on the use of turmeric in 
wound healing was challenged. The said patent was also cancelled. 
 Limited claims of the patent on Basmati Ricelines and grains granted in the United 
States of America have also been challenged. 
 In order to protect bio-resources, the Patents (Second Amendment) Bill 1999, 
contains provisions for mandatory disclosure of source and geographical origin of the biological 
material used in the invention while applying fo r patents in India. Provisions have also been 
incorporated to include the non-disclosure or wrongful disclosure of the same as gr ounds for 
opposition and for revocation of the patent, if granted. Provisions in this regard are contained in 
clauses 8, 17 and 28 of the said Bill. 
 In order to protect traditional knowledge fro m being patented, provisions have been 
incorporated in the Patents (Second Amendment)  Bill,  1999,  to  include  anticipation of 
invention  by

available local knowledge, including oral knowledge, as one of the grounds for opposition 
as also for revocation of patent. Provisions in this regard are contained in clauses 17 and 28 
of the said Bill.

database of traditional knowledge in the field of  medicinal plants to avoid patenting of such 
knowledge.

 1583. SHRI SURESH KALMADI:  
     SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI:  
 Will the Minister of DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government have appointed global advisors for disinvestment in various

(b) if so, the details of the criteria for their selection; and

 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF TH E DEPARTMENT OF DISINVESTMENT 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) Yes, sir. 'Advisors' have been appointed. 
(b) The selection of the Advisors is based on the process of Global Competitive 
Selection in which both Indian & International consultants are eligible to bid. The procedure 
involves issuing advertis ments, both nationally and interna tionally, as per the transaction 
requirements, calling the bidder s to make presentations be fore an inter ministerial 
Committee, evaluation of their presentations on a predetermined criteria, short listing on the 
basis of evaluation and selection of the lowe st bidder among the short listed parties. The

capabilities, personnel, infrastructure and investment in India. Understanding of the-PSU to 
be disinvested, team of Advisors, Proposed valuation and methodogy suggested etc.

payable to the advisors, genera lly consist of two components. The first component is called 
'success fee' which is

                                                     RAJYA SABHA            [7August, 2000] 
fixed percentage of the gross proceeds to be received by the Government from the 
disinvestment. Since it is di rectly linked with the amount  of money realisible from 
disinvestment, it serves as an incentive to the Advisor to get the best price from 
disinvestment. 
 The other component of the fee is called 'drop dead fee' which is lump sum 
amount payable to the advisor only in the even t of the transaction being called off by the 
Government.

Increase in Drug Abuse 
 1649. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the number of people affected by drug abuse is on the 
increase; 
(b) whether the main section of population affected by this drug abuse belong to the 
poor section of our society; 
(c) whether India is not merely a transit country for illicit drug traffic but is also 
becoming a significant consumer; and 
(d) if so, the steps Government have taken to deal with this menace and how 
effective they have been? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI ): (a) to (c) The different 
studies and reports indicate to an increas ing incidence of drug abuse amongst certain 
marginalized/vulnerable sections of the society including street children, commercial sex 
workers, transport workers, slum dwellers, opium growing regions, border areas etc. To that 
extent it is a reported fact that the numbe r of people affected by drug abuse is on the 
increase and population affected belong to poor sections of our society and India is also 
becoming a consumer. 
 (d) Recognizing drug abuse as psycho-soci o-medical problem, which can be best 
handled in community settings, the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment has been 
implementing the Scheme for Prevention of Alcoholism and Substance (Drugs) Abuse. 
Under the Scheme, grant in aid is provided to  the voluntary organisations for implementing 
community-based programmes on awareness generation, preventive education, counseling 
and identification, detoxification,  rehabilitation and after-care of the addicts. At the end of 
the cyar 1999-2000, the Ministry provided assistance to 368 organizations for operating 452 
centres, (160 counselling and Awareness centr es and 292 Treatment-cum-Rehabilitation 
centres) all over the country. The Ministry of health and Family Welfare are also supporting  
around  90  De-addiction  centres  through  Government 
181 

                                                       RAJYA SABHA [7 August, 2000] 
hospitals. Besides the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment has been utilizing media 
channels-electronic and print—for disse minating information amongst the masses.

Welfare of Blinds 
 1654. SHRI RAMACHANDRAIAH RUMA NDLA: Will the Minister of 
SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the allocation made for welfare of blinds; 
(b) whether it is a fact that only 8 to 10 per cent of blind children get basic school 
education in view of limited funding; and 
(c) if so, the action proposed to grant more funds for welfare of blinds? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GAN DHI): (a) There is no separate 
budget provision for visual disability. During the current financial year, 2000-01, a 
provision of Rs. 230.10 crore (Plan) and Rs. 31.05 crore (Non-Plan) has been provided in 
the budget of the Ministry of Social Justic e and Empowerment for the disability sector, 
including visual disability. In adition, Rs.31.70  crore (Plan) is earmarked for North-East 
region for this sector. 
 (b) and (c) Complete data of school going visually handicapped children is not 
available. According to the National Institut e for the Visualy Handicapped, out of a total 
2,00,000 estimated poplulation of school-going age visually handicappe d children, it is 
normally held that 8 to 10% are getting basic school education. However, this coverage of 
visually handicaped children cannot be attributed to limited funding only. There are other 
factors, such as, (a) Reluctance on the part of parents to send a girl blind child to school due 
to social stigma; (b) Lack of awareness on the part of parents and th eir over protection; and 
(c) Location of residential schools—there are ma ny districts in the country not having even 
a single residential school for the blind thereby denying accessibility to such schools. 
 Schemes to promote special edu cation, including, special schools.
